landmarks.name: Lope National Park
landmarks.writeup: A UNESCO World Heritage site known for its biodiversity and mix of savanna and rainforest ecosystems.

wiki.extract: Lopé National Park is a national park in central Gabon. Bordered by the Ogooué River to the north and the Chaillu Massif to the south, the park has an area of 4,912 km2 (1,897 sq mi).

landmarks.name: Belinga Iron Ore Mine
landmarks.writeup: One of the largest iron ore deposits in Africa, significant for Gabon's mining industry.

wiki.extract: Fortescue is a global metal mining company headquartered in Australia. Fortescue focused on iron ore mining under the name of Fortescue Metals Group (FMG) until July 2023. As of 2017, Fortescue is the fourth-largest iron ore producer in the world. The company has holdings of more than 87,000 km2 in the Pilbara region of Western Australia, making it the largest tenement holder in the state, larger than both BHP and Rio Tinto.

landmarks.name: Libreville Cathedral
landmarks.writeup: A prominent religious site and architectural landmark in Gabon's capital.

wiki.extract: Libreville is the capital and largest city of Gabon, located on the Gabon Estuary. Libreville occupies 65 square kilometres (25 sq mi) of the northwestern province of Estuaire. Libreville is also a port on the Gabon Estuary, near the Gulf of Guinea. As of the 2013 census, its population was 703,904.

landmarks.name: Ivindo National Park
landmarks.writeup: Famous for its waterfalls, including the Kongou Falls, and rich wildlife.

wiki.extract: Ivindo National Park is a national park in east-central Gabon in Central Africa, straddling the border of the Ogooué-Ivindo and Ogooué-Lolo provinces. Its creation was announced in August 2002 by then-President Omar Bongo at the Earth Summit in Johannesburg, along with Gabon's 12 other terrestrial national parks. Most famous for the spectacular Kongou and Mingouli waterfalls of the Ivindo River, known as the “wonders of Ivindo”, the park also includes the Ipassa Makokou Biosphere Reserve and Langoué Baï, one of the 5 most important forest clearings in Central Africa. The park was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 for its outstanding biodiversity and relatively intact tropical forest ecosystem.

cultural_events.name: Bwiti Festival
cultural_events.writeup: A traditional spiritual ceremony involving music, dance, and the use of the iboga plant.

wiki.extract: Music of Gabon encompasses the traditional, ritual, popular and urban musics of the Gabonese Republic. Scholarly literature describes Gabonese musical life as highly diverse, reflecting the country's ethnolinguistic plurality, especially Fang, Myènè, Teke, Punu, Njebi, Kota, Mitsogo and Babongo/Bongo communities, and the close historical connection between music, dance, healing, initiation and oral literature.

cultural_events.name: Fang New Year
cultural_events.writeup: Celebration marking the new year with traditional dances and rituals among the Fang people.

wiki.extract: Fang Fang, pen name of Wang Fang, is a Chinese writer, known for her literary depictions of the working poor. She won the Lu Xun Literary Prize in 2010. Born in Nanjing, she attended Wuhan University in 1978 to study Chinese. In 1975, she began to write poetry and in 1982, her first novel was published. She has since written several novels, some of which have been honored by Chinese national-level literary prizes. Fang garnered international attention for her Wuhan Diary, documenting the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic in China, and has used her platform to call for an end to internet censorship in China.

cultural_events.name: Gabon Independence Day
cultural_events.writeup: National holiday on August 17 celebrating Gabon's independence from France in 1960.

wiki.extract: An Independence Day is an annual event commemorating the anniversary of a nation's independence or statehood, usually after ceasing to be a group or part of another nation or state, or after the end of a military occupation, or after a major change in government. Many countries commemorate their independence from a colonial empire.

food_writeup: Gabonese cuisine features ingredients like cassava, plantains, fish, and bushmeat, with dishes often flavored with palm oil and spices reflecting Central African culinary traditions.
brief_history: Gabon was inhabited by Pygmy peoples before Bantu migrations. It became a French colony in the 19th century and gained independence in 1960. Since then, it has been politically stable with an economy reliant on oil, mining, and timber.
current_conflicts: Gabon is generally stable with no significant internal or external conflicts reported as of 2024.

commentary.inflation_management: Gabon's inflation has been low throughout, anchored by the Central African CFA franc's peg to the euro: it peaked at 5.3% in 2008 and troughed at -1.4% in 2006, averaging around 2%. Even the 2022 global shock produced only 4.3%, easing to a projected 2.0% in 2025. The BEAC's regional monetary policy has delivered exemplary price stability through coups, oil crashes, and pandemics. But as in other CEMAC oil states, the peg's stability conceals a competitiveness problem: with oil in long-term decline as a share of output, the real exchange rate offers no cushion for diversification, and adjustment falls entirely on fiscal policy.
commentary.debt_management: Gabon's debt tracks oil with a ratchet effect: it falls in booms and jumps in busts, never fully returning. From 20.1% of GDP in 2008 it rose after the 2014 oil crash to 63.9% by 2016, then COVID and a second oil shock drove it to 83.0% in 2020, the series high. The 2021-22 oil rebound brought only partial relief (66.4% in 2022), and renewed borrowing plus weaker oil pushed it back to a projected 78.6% in 2025. Gabon has issued Eurobonds and borrowed from China; IMF programs have pressed for consolidation with limited success. The structural problem is a public wage bill and spending level built for $100 oil in a $70-80 world.

key_events.event: Omar Bongo died after 42 years in power; son Ali Bongo succeeded him.
Oil price crash ended the boom; debt began its climb from 34.3% of GDP.
Disputed re-election of Ali Bongo triggered violent protests; a 2019 coup attempt failed.
COVID-19 and oil crash pushed debt to 83.0% of GDP, the series high.
August 30, 2023: military ousted Ali Bongo after a disputed election, ending 56 years of Bongo rule; General Brice Oligui Nguema took power.
April 12, 2025: Oligui won the presidential election with about 90% of the vote, formalizing the transition.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued oil dependence with debt near 80% of GDP and low inflation under the CFA peg. Upside depends on whether the new government diversifies (manganese, timber processing) and controls the wage bill; downside is another oil downturn forcing abrupt adjustment. Uncertainty is moderate: the 2023-25 transition was orderly by regional standards, but the economic model is unchanged and oil output is mature.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
